Coral reefs are often described as the "rainforests of the sea" due to their extraordinary biodiversity and ecological significance. To understand their importance, one must first appreciate the complex biological process behind their formation. Contrary to popular belief, corals are not plants or rocks, but rather colonies of tiny, soft-bodied animals known as polyps. These polyps live in symbiotic relationships with microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which reside within the coral tissues. This partnership is the engine of reef growth. The algae perform photosynthesis, converting sunlight, carbon dioxide, and nutrients into energy and oxygen, which they share with the host coral. In return, the coral provides the algae with a protected environment and the compounds they need to carry out photosynthesis.

The physical structure of a reef is built through a process of calcification. The coral polyps extract calcium carbonate from the surrounding seawater to build hard, protective exoskeletons around their soft bodies. When a polyp dies, its skeleton remains, and new polyps settle on top of it, continuing the cycle. Over centuries and even millennia, these layers of calcium carbonate accumulate, forming the massive, intricate structures we recognize as coral reefs.
